sentences.text: Every day, people post their locations, opinions, and private moments for the world to see.
Some people claim that because people increasingly feel compelled to share personal details online, the right to privacy is eroding.
I largely agree that privacy is under threat, but I believe it is not lost and can still be protected.
First, it is true that constant online sharing is weakening privacy.
People now reveal details about their lives that earlier generations kept strictly private.
For example, photos, locations, and opinions posted online can be seen and stored by countless strangers.
This shows that the line between private and public life is fading fast.
Companies and governments can also gather huge amounts of personal data from what we share.
Once information is online, it can be almost impossible to take back.
To this extent, the claim points to a real and growing danger.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why privacy can still be protected

sentences.text: Second, however, the right to privacy is not lost and can still be defended.
People can choose how much to share and can learn to protect their own information.
Consider how strong laws and better settings can limit who sees our personal data.
Such tools show that privacy can be protected even in a connected world.
Many people are also becoming more careful and demanding greater control over their data.
The fact that some people overshare does not mean privacy must disappear for all.
Privacy, then, is threatened but far from beyond saving.
In conclusion, constant online sharing truly is eroding our privacy.
But the right to privacy is not lost, since laws and careful habits can still defend it.
Privacy will survive only if we choose to protect it rather than give it away freely.
